newsitem.title: UK: Britain urged to set up N.Irish parades watchdog.
newsitem.headline: Britain urged to set up N.Irish parades watchdog.

text.p: Britain was urged by an independent body on Thursday to set up a watchdog to defuse sectarian tension during Northern Ireland's Protestant "marching season."

The Independent Review of Parades and Marches, set up after clashes swept the province last summer, said a five-person "parades commission," rather than the police, should decide whether marches near Catholic areas should in effect be banned.
But the largely Protestant police would have the right of appeal if they believed public order was endangered.
"We recommend that the Parades Commission keeps under review the potential difficulty of significant clashes between parades and open-air public meetings," the team said.

"We recommend that the responsibility for reaching conclusions in relation to disputed parades should in future be that of the Parades Commission rather than the RUC (police)", the report team chaired by British academic Peter North said.
The report was published on the 25th anniversary of Bloody Sunday when 13 Catholics on a civil rights march were shot dead by British troops in Londonderry.

The commission said the Royal Ulster Constabulary would be empowered to appeal to the government against a commission decision and the final say about preserving order should rest with the police, the report said.

"We recommend that in the extreme circumstances of the determination of the Parades Commission being defied, the police should retain the power to intervene on public order grounds as a parade is assembling or proceeding."

Protestants deny Catholic charges of bigotry and say their annual marches show their loyality to their faith and the British Crown. Catholics regard them as triumphalist commemorations of 300-year-old victories over the native Irish.

Two people were killed and many injured during a summer frenzy of sectarian violence in 1996. Hangover effects are seen in arson attacks on churches and boycotts of Catholic and Protestant traders in some rural communities.

The vortex of the trouble was in the town of Portadown 25 miles (35km) south of Belfast. Police banned the Orange Order from parading through a Catholic area but reversed the decision three days later after province-wide Protestant protests.
On July 12 a large force of police and soldiers hemmed Catholics into their side-streets to allow a march of some 500 Orangemen along Belfast's Lower Ormeau Road.
North told a press conference after his report was published: "Many of those we talked to told us of their alarm at the potential consequences of the disruption last summer.
"We can only hope that, in these recommendations, people will recognise another way forward. Parades and protests have the capability of polarising communities, as we have seen."
Leaked details of the report last week were broadly welcomed by the largely Protestant RUC, many of whom complained about being caught in the middle of opposing factions last year.
But Jeffrey Donaldson, a leader of the Orange Order, the main pro-British marching fraternity, said a commission would become "a factory of grievance".
Catholic groups reacted cautiously. Sources in the Catholic community said they did not expect the plans to be a panacea.

Northern Ireland has been plagued by a series of bombings in recent weeks. The Irish Republican Army, seeking a united Ireland, broke its September 1994 ceasefire in February but Protestant guerrillas have held to theirs.
